newsitem.title: UK: Mark soft in Europe amid EMU optimism, buoyant dlr.
newsitem.headline: Mark soft in Europe amid EMU optimism, buoyant dlr.

text.p: The mark was soft on its European crosses by midday trade, testing two-month lows against the lira and peseta, amid positive EMU sentiment spawned at the week-end Ecofin meeting in the Netherlands and the dollar's gains against the mark.

At the weekend meeting, European finance ministers set a late-April, early-May 1998 date for a decision on first wave EMU participants as well as agreeing details on stability pact fines and sanctions.
Agreement was also reached on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism linking the euro to those outside first-wave participation.

"Threshing out details that needed sorting out, particularly on when and for how long EMU fines will be applicable, has lifted the overall impression of uncertainty hanging over the single currency," Credit Lyonnais economist David Thwaites said.

The market shrugged off German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's opposition to a loose interpretation of EMU debt criteria, contrary to UK press reports which quoted him as saying he had never nailed himself to the cross of three percent.
"Three percent is three percent and it will stay that way," he said. However, German government officials stressed that Waigel's "three percent" did not mean "3.0" percent as seen in earlier reports.

"It seems like he's trying to have the best of both worlds. On the one hand saying he is willing to be flexible, and on the other saying that's not what he meant," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"I think his first comment (about Waigel saying he never nailed to cross of three percent) is the most likely, it's a truer reflection of what will actually happen."
Mark/Lira slipped to near two-month lows and was trading at 985.80/6.00 lire at 1018 GMT compared with 990.70/95 lire late Friday in Europe.
Mark/peseta was also lower and stood at 84.45/47 against 84.51/52 pesetas on Friday.
The mark also lost ground against a stronger dollar which breached the 1.70 mark and 125 yen levels by midday trade, buoyed by the prospect of further U.S. rate hikes.
However, dealers said overall trade was cautious in Europe ahead of the German March jobless data on Tuesday.

"We're expecting German jobless data to show a drop between 200,000 and 230,000," Thwaites said. "Figures for March-May should be good due to the weather, and will add to the impression that Germany is turning the corner."
Strong economic data from Germany, the single currency linchpin, would in turn boost hopes that EMU will go ahead on time in 1999.
